title: CD84 is a specific target for acute myeloid leukemia CAR-T cell therapy
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 08 May 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-72361-4

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has been shown successful in a range of malignancies but due to an absence of notable antigenic targets has limited its application to acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Here the authors identify CD84 as a potential target for AML and show that the application of CD84 CAR-T in models of AML results in reduced tumour burden and enhanced survival.
headline: Scientists found a new target on leukemia cells that allows immune cells to attack them more effectively.
why_it_matters: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a deadly blood cancer that has been hard to treat with a promising new therapy called CAR-T cells. This discovery opens the door to using CAR-T therapy for AML patients who currently have limited options. If this works in human trials, it could give thousands of AML patients a new chance at survival.
key_findings: CD84 is a protein found on AML cells that can be recognized as a target by CAR-T cells (immune cells that have been reprogrammed to hunt down cancer)
When researchers created CAR-T cells designed to recognize CD84, these cells successfully killed AML cancer cells in laboratory and animal models
Mice treated with CD84-targeting CAR-T cells showed reduced tumor growth and lived longer than untreated mice
CD84 appears to be specific to blood cancer cells, meaning the therapy might avoid harming healthy cells
methods_snapshot: The team identified CD84 as a target by analyzing which proteins are present on AML cells. They then created CAR-T cells (by taking immune cells and genetically modifying them to display a 'recognition receptor' for CD84) and tested how well these cells killed cancer in laboratory dishes and in mice.

glossary.definition: A treatment where a patient's immune cells are removed, engineered in a lab to recognize and attack cancer, then returned to the patient's body
A fast-growing blood cancer that starts in cells that normally develop into white blood cells
A protein found on the surface of AML cells that can act as a marker for immune cells to identify and attack
A molecule on a cell's surface that the immune system can recognize as a target
An engineered receptor placed on immune cells that allows them to recognize and attack specific cancer cells

limitations: This research was done in laboratory dishes and mice, not yet in human patients, so we don't know if the same success will translate to people. The long-term safety and whether healthy blood cells might also be affected remain to be tested in clinical trials.
